availability.body: Unlike running or cycling, swimming requires infrastructure: a pool, or natural water with the right conditions. Pools are expensive to build and operate, are typically municipal, and keep limited hours. Natural water in a temperate climate like Sweden's averages 13–17 °C even at the July peak — cold enough that most of the year it is simply not an option — and open water brings currents, algae blooms and cold shock on top of absent supervision.
availability.title: Availability

section1.conclusionBody: bathing is double-edged. The pleasure, the calm and the exercise are real; so are the financial, hygienic, safety and availability barriers. The goal of Aquafulness is to recreate some of the most anticipated positive effects of bathing without the immersion — available at any hour, in any weather, to anyone with a screen.

cost.body: Entry fees to Swedish public baths have risen markedly with inflation and energy prices — typically 70–200 SEK per adult visit, with season passes at 1,500–3,000 SEK. Even with discounts for students, retirees and prescription-based physical activity (FaR), prices are prohibitive for many.
cost.title: Cost

dressCodes.body: Hygiene and safety rules restrict pool clothing to swimwear textiles (lycra/spandex), since ordinary cotton clothing sheds particles, carries germs and — heavy with water — increases drowning risk. At the same time, a growing share of guests prefer, for religious, cultural or neurodiversity reasons, swimwear that covers the body more fully. The resulting tension has been genuinely contentious; facilities increasingly respond with full-cover swimwear (such as the burkini) available for hire, and with dedicated quiet or group-specific hours.
dressCodes.title: Dress codes and inclusivity

hygiene.body: Shared water and shared facilities (locker rooms, floors, furniture) carry infection risks ranging from skin conditions to serious waterborne illness. The chlorine used to control germs brings its own concerns for regular bathers and for staff.
hygiene.title: Hygiene

overcrowding.body: Because bathing is so popular, facilities and beaches crowd heavily outside office hours and on holidays — raising germ loads, collision and drowning risk, and noise that itself excludes people who find crowds difficult.
overcrowding.title: Overcrowding

section1.p1: Bathing is a rare kind of activity. Immersion in warm water engages many senses at once and, unlike most physical activity, produces sensations of calm, relaxation, weightlessness and gentle massage. For many people, time in the water is a cornerstone of well-being, and swimming has long been among the most popular of all leisure activities.
section1.p2: But the case study behind Aquafulness catalogues an equally long list of barriers and downsides to real-world bathing:

safety.body: Drowning is the most serious danger of water, in pools and open water alike. Rescue that comes too late — or almost too late — can mean death or lifelong disability. This is why pools are staffed with lifeguards, enforce dress codes, and cap the number of bathers.
safety.title: Safety

section1.title: Why bathe digitally?

travel.body: Chasing warm water abroad — Gran Canaria, Thailand, Mallorca — costs a Swedish household roughly 28,000–150,000 SEK for a week, increasingly financed on credit. Add visas, insurance against catastrophic hospital bills, unfamiliar legal systems, intense sun, and ocean hazards from rip currents to stinging aquatic life. The case study also notes that the geopolitical shocks of the 2020s — the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, escalation in the Middle East — have made travel abroad riskier and less certain than it has been in decades.
travel.title: Travel

audiovisual.body: what works best. Sound and image reinforce each other, so neither channel has to carry the experience alone.

auditory.body: the most common method historically, from 1980s field-recording cassettes of ocean waves to modern generative soundscape apps. Effective, but it still leans on imagination to fill in the picture, which carries cognitive cost.

section2.conclusion: Aquafulness is built on the audiovisual combination.

imagination.body: the most primitive method. It works, but demands freedom from distraction and is cognitively expensive; it succeeds best when the person is already relaxed.

section3.p1: The case study then asks the deeper question: what actually is the soothing thing about water?
section3.p2After: . The felt qualities of calm warm water — weightlessness, smoothness, the sense of being held, carried, and cared for, perhaps rooted as far back as prenatal experience — all share one physical signature: the flow and force of calm water is a sinusoidal oscillation. Whether you watch water move, hear it lap, or feel it carry you, the stimulus arriving at the senses is smooth, periodic, and predictable. The theory is that this oscillation entrains the observer toward the same calm.

section4.p1: From theory to design, the solution is stated plainly in the case study:
section4.quote: Create an audiovisual digital experience that resembles the point of view of a bather immersed in a warm lake. Emphasize the colors — the light-brown-to-blue nature of real water — and let that image be an overlay to a visual where the projection smoothly moves like a wave, to induce a kinesthetic perception of being immersed in water which flows with you back and forward — the sense of being cared for, the bobbing movement.
steps: A first-person camera placed at bather height in an ocean or lake scene.
The camera's position driven by smooth periodic motion, rocking the entire rendered image the way a floating body rocks.
Water surfaces whose vertices and textures move in slow sinusoidal waves, in natural water colors.
Ocean and wind audio loops underneath.

opticFlow.disclaimerBody: this page describes design reasoning, grounded in the personal experience of the project's creator and in generally known perceptual concepts used here as inspiration. It makes no medical claims. Aquafulness has not been clinically evaluated; nothing below asserts a therapeutic effect, and individual experience will vary.

furtherReading.after: for real, peer-reviewed studies with Harvard citations and PubMed/DOI links.
furtherReading.before: The terms used above — optic flow, vection, and slow vestibular ("heave") stimulation — are established in the perception and sleep-science literature, though not tested on Aquafulness itself. See

section1.p1After: — is that sight and sound, done right, can cue the memory of the rest. The brain that has floated in a warm lake knows what that full sensory bundle feels like; a sufficiently evocative audiovisual fragment invites it to fill in the remainder.
section1.p1Before: Real bathing is multisensory: skin temperature, buoyancy relieving the joints, hydrostatic pressure, the vestibular signal of being rocked, the sound of water, the sight of it. A screen and a speaker can address only two of those channels. The bet Aquafulness makes — the case study calls it
section1.p2: The question is what "done right" means. Aquafulness's answer has three parts: coherent optic flow, whole-field oscillation, and the sine wave as the common signature of calm water.
section1.title: The design problem

layer1.body: The camera's height rides a smooth periodic oscillation, so every pixel of the rendered image translates up and down together, with the smooth acceleration profile of a real swell. Whole-field coherent motion is exactly the stimulus class the visual system treats as evidence of self-motion rather than object motion.

layer2.body: The water's texture and displacement drift slowly and continuously across the surface. This is the classic laminar flow pattern of water moving past a floating observer — unhurried, uniform, endless. There is no destination and no event; the flow signals only that the water is alive and carrying you.

layer3.body: The water surface itself rises and falls in an interference pattern of overlapping waves — in this app, a sum of sinusoids sampled from a directional wave spectrum — so nearby crests and far troughs move in the counter-phased way real swell does, giving the flow field believable depth structure rather than a flat scroll.

section2.p1Body: is the pattern of motion across the entire visual field that an observer experiences as they — or their surroundings — move. It is one of the strongest visual cues the brain uses to work out its own motion: a flow field expanding from a point ahead reads as moving forward; the whole scene translating gently upward reads as you sinking, and downward as rising.
section2.p2: Aquafulness constructs its optic flow from three layers:
section2.p3Before: Together these produce the specific optic-flow diet of a bather: global, slow, periodic, coherent. Nothing in the scene moves abruptly; nothing demands a saccade; nothing violates the prediction the last few seconds established. In the vocabulary of the case study, the visual channel is being fed a
section2.title: Optic flow: the visual signature of moving through water

section3.bullet1After: , not to objects in the scene, so the induced interpretation is "my body is bobbing," not "that buoy is bobbing."
section3.bullet1Before: The rocking is applied to the
section3.bullet2: The bob sits at the tempo of a slow, comfortable swell — the rhythm of a hammock or a slowly rocked cradle rather than of chop or turbulence. Slow rocking of this kind is widely associated, in everyday experience, with soothing; the case study grounds it more personally, in the feeling of being held and cared for, speculating that it may root as deep as prenatal experience.
section3.bullet3: Wave height, speed and style are user-adjustable in the app's settings, because comfort thresholds differ — the same motion that reads as delicious swaying to one person is too much for another.
section3.p1After: — the compelling illusion of self-motion in the absence of any physical movement (the railway-carriage effect: the train beside yours pulls away and you feel you are moving). Vection is the bridge from watching water to feeling carried by it.
section3.p1Before: When a large portion of the visual field moves coherently, observers commonly experience
section3.p2: Aquafulness is deliberately built to invite a gentle, oscillatory vection:
section3.p3After: here means the felt sense of one's own body's position and motion: the goal is not that the user judges the water looks nice, but that their body, at some level, feels rocked.
section3.p3Before: The case study names the intended result directly: the projection moving smoothly like a wave should "induce a kinesthetic perception of being immersed in water which flows with you back and forward" — the bobbing movement, the sense of being cared for.
section3.p4: Two design choices support comfort in this induced motion:

predictability.body: Sinusoidal motion is maximally predictable — the brain locks onto the rhythm within a cycle or two, so the visual-vestibular mismatch (the eyes report rocking, the inner ear reports stillness) stays gentle and expected. Erratic or accelerating motion with the same mismatch is what tends toward discomfort; a pure slow sine is about the mildest possible form of it.

stableFrame.body: On a phone or laptop screen, the device's bezel and the room beyond remain visible and stationary, which naturally limits vection to a pleasant, partial sensation rather than a destabilizing one. A fully enclosing display is correspondingly the setting where the floating illusion can become strongest.

section3.title: Vection and kinesthetic movement: seeing motion, feeling motion

section4.p1: Why should any of this be calming? The case study's reasoning, offered as personal theory:
section4.p2After: — the unhurried rocking, the living surface, the water light — for the many situations where real bathing is out of reach: the wrong hour, the wrong season, the wrong budget, a crowded pool, a body or mind that finds the facility difficult, or simply a five-minute pause at a desk.
section4.p2Before: The purpose, then, is modest and specific:
section4.p2Emphasis: to recreate, through visualization, the calming of bathing

reason1.body: The sight of open water — the popularly termed "blue mind" observation — is soothing to most people, independent of any illusion of motion. Aquafulness leans into this with its natural palette: the light-brown-to-blue colors of a real lake or ocean, warm tones under translucent blue-green water, a saturation-lifted sky.
reason1.term: Watching water is calming in itself.

reason2.body: Everything a calm bath presents to the senses — the swell you feel, the lapping you hear, the flow you see — is smooth periodic oscillation. The theory is that presenting this same signature through the available channels (eyes and ears) entrains the observer toward the state the full-immersion version produces: the state the case study coins "aquaful."
reason2.term: The common denominator of calm water is the sine wave.

reason3.body: The experience is composed to match the memory of a specific, good place — floating in warm, open water. Sound reinforces sight: ocean and wind audio supply the auditory sine bed so the visuals don't have to carry the association alone. This is the audiovisual combination the case study identifies as the most effective seeding method — stronger than sound alone, which still taxes the imagination, and far cheaper cognitively than imagination alone.

section4.title: The calming purpose: recreating the bath

section5.p1: It bears repeating outside the disclaimer: Aquafulness does not claim to lower blood pressure, treat anxiety, replace exercise, or produce any measured clinical effect. It is a visualization built on one person's careful attention to why bathing feels the way it does, and on well-worn perceptual ideas — optic flow, vection, the soothing quality of slow rhythm — used as craft, the way a filmmaker uses them, not as medicine. If it gives you three minutes of the ocean in the middle of winter, it has done its job.
section5.title: What this is not

citations.text: Wright, W.G., DiZio, P. and Lackner, J.R. (2005) 'Vertical linear self-motion perception during visual and inertial motion: more than weighted summation of sensory inputs', Journal of Vestibular Research, 15(4), pp. 185–195.
Nakamura, S., Palmisano, S. and Kim, J. (2016) 'Relative visual oscillation can facilitate visually induced self-motion perception', i-Perception, 7(4), pp. 1–18. doi: 10.1177/2041669516661903.

Wang, W., Yang, K. and Zhu, Y. (2021) 'Optimal frequency and amplitude of vertical viewpoint oscillation for improving vection strength and reducing neural constraints on gait', Entropy, 23(5), 541. doi: 10.3390/e23050541.

Nooij, S.A.E., Pretto, P. and Bülthoff, H.H. (2018) 'More vection means more velocity storage activity: a factor in visually induced motion sickness?', Experimental Brain Research, 236(11), pp. 3031–3041. doi: 10.1007/s00221-018-5340-1.

groups.note: Together these show that oscillatory visual motion alone — without any physical movement — induces the perception of self-motion, that vertical viewpoint oscillation (the app's "whole-field rocking") measurably strengthens that illusion, and, as a caveat, that stronger vection is also linked to a higher risk of visually induced motion sickness — why the app keeps motion slow and user-adjustable rather than maximizing vection strength.
groups.title: Optic flow, vection and self-motion perception

citations.text: Yang, A.H.X., Khwaounjoo, P. and Cakmak, Y.O. (2021) 'Directional effects of whole-body spinning and visual flow in virtual reality on vagal neuromodulation', Journal of Vestibular Research, 31(6), pp. 479–494. doi: 10.3233/VES-201574.

Kuldavletova, O., Denise, P., Normand, H., Quarck, G. and Etard, O.M. (2023) 'Both whole-body rotation and visual flow induce cardiovascular autonomic response in human, but visual response is overridden by vestibular stimulation', Scientific Reports, 13, 4191. doi: 10.1038/s41598-023-31431-z.

groups.note: Both studies find that optic flow alone — with no physical motion — measurably shifts vagal/parasympathetic activity, the physiological substrate of the "calming" claim made about coherent visual flow.
groups.title: Visual flow and autonomic (vagal/parasympathetic) response

citations.text: Bayer, L., Constantinescu, I., Perrig, S., Vienne, J., Vidal, P.-P., Mühlethaler, M. and Schwartz, S. (2011) 'Rocking synchronizes brain waves during a short nap', Current Biology, 21(12), pp. R461–R462. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2011.05.012.

Omlin, X., Crivelli, F., Näf, M., Heinicke, L., Skorucak, J., Malafeev, A., Fernandez Guerrero, A., Riener, R. and Achermann, P. (2018) 'The effect of a slowly rocking bed on sleep', Scientific Reports, 8, 2156. doi: 10.1038/s41598-018-19880-3.

Perrault, A.A., Khani, A., Quairiaux, C., Kompotis, K., Franken, P., Mühlethaler, M., Schwartz, S. and Bayer, L. (2019) 'Whole-night continuous rocking entrains spontaneous neural oscillations with benefits for sleep and memory', Current Biology, 29(3), pp. 402–411.e3. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2018.12.028.

van Sluijs, R.M., Rondei, Q.J., Schluep, D., Jäger, L., Riener, R., Achermann, P. and Wilhelm, E. (2020) 'Effect of rocking movements on afternoon sleep', Frontiers in Neuroscience, 13, 1446. doi: 10.3389/fnins.2019.01446.

Subramaniam, A., Eberhard-Moscicka, A.K., Ertl, M. and Mast, F.W. (2023) 'Rocking devices and the role of vestibular stimulation on sleep — a systematic review', Clinical and Translational Neuroscience, 7(4), 40. doi: 10.3390/ctn7040040.

groups.note: These studies are the direct evidence base for the app's central analogy: slow (roughly 0.25 Hz), passive rocking — the same low-frequency vertical "heave" motion the camera applies to the whole visual field — measurably promotes relaxation, faster sleep onset and deeper sleep in humans, and is understood to work through rhythmic vestibular stimulation.
groups.title: Rocking, vestibular ("heave") stimulation, sleep and relaxation

citations.text: Ulrich, R.S., Simons, R.F., Losito, B.D., Fiorito, E., Miles, M.A. and Zelson, M. (1991) 'Stress recovery during exposure to natural and urban environments', Journal of Environmental Psychology, 11(3), pp. 201–230. doi: 10.1016/S0272-4944(05)80184-7.

White, M.P., Smith, A., Humphryes, K., Pahl, S., Snelling, D. and Depledge, M. (2010) 'Blue space: the importance of water for preference, affect, and restorativeness ratings of natural and built scenes', Journal of Environmental Psychology, 30(4), pp. 482–493. doi: 10.1016/j.jenvp.2010.04.004.

groups.note: The foundational Ulrich study shows that video of natural scenes produces faster physiological stress recovery than video of urban scenes; White et al. found that scenes containing water are rated higher for preference, positive affect and perceived restorativeness than equivalent scenes without water — direct empirical grounding for the "blue mind"/watching-water effect, independent of any motion illusion.
groups.title: Watching water and stress recovery ("blue mind")

references.intro: Real, peer-reviewed studies related to the perceptual concepts referenced on the previous pages — optic flow, vection, and low-frequency (rocking/"heave") vestibular stimulation — and to the "blue mind" observation about watching water. Citations use Harvard style, with a PubMed/PMC or publisher DOI link for each.
references.scopeNoteBody: No study listed here was conducted on Aquafulness, and none tests a floating ocean visualization specifically. They establish the component perceptual and physiological effects — that coherent optic flow and vection can be generated visually, that slow rocking/vestibular stimulation is associated with relaxation and sleep onset, and that looking at water and nature scenes is associated with stress recovery — that the design combines by analogy. As the disclaimers elsewhere in this app state, this is design reasoning grounded in existing literature and personal experience, not a clinical claim about Aquafulness itself.
references.title: Scientific References
